stories.title: US cancels joint marine drills with South Korea over Iran war-related force constraints
stories.summary: The allies remain in close consultations on resuming the drills.
article_sentences: The US cancelled the September joint amphibious landing drill with South Korea due to limited US force availability linked to the Iran war.
The US Marine Corps informed South Korea in June about these constraints, while both sides are discussing ways to resume the exercises.
North Korea condemned the drills, firing missiles recently, and US President Trump had already scaled back other joint exercises citing hostility concerns and costs.

The United States cancelled a joint amphibious landing drill scheduled for September with South Korea, Seoul’s Marine Corps said on Aug 24, after Washington cited constraints on the availability of US forces due to the war in Iran.

The US Marine Corps formally notified its South Korean counterpart in June that force availability would be constrained for the division-level exercise, known as Ssangyong, a South Korean Marine Corps spokesperson told a press briefing.
The allies remain in close consultations on resuming the drills, the spokesperson said.
He did not specify what measures might be taken to prevent future cancellations or to make up for lost training opportunities.
US Forces Korea did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The cancellation follows US President Donald Trump’s surprise order to scale back a separate annual joint military exercise that ended on Aug 21, citing the cost and Seoul’s refusal to take part in the Iran war.
Trump also wrote on his Truth Social platform that the Ulchi Freedom Shield drills sent “a signal that was totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J.
Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful.”
Despite the reduction of the exercises, Pyongyang fired 10 short-range ballistic missiles last week and issued a statement denouncing the exercises.

stories.title: Gauff, Fils win Cincinnati tennis titles in run-up to US Open
stories.summary: Gauff beat Pegula for her second Cincinnati Open trophy and Fils overcame Tiafoe for his first Masters 1000 title. Coco Gauff has defeated fellow American Jessica Pegula, 6-2, 6-4, to capture her second women’s Cincinnati Open title as she looks ahead to the US Open starting in New York next week. Arthur Fils of France overcame American Frances Tiafoe 6-3, 1-6, 6-0, in the men’s final for his first Masters 1000 title, with Sunday’s decider marking the first time two Black players competed in an ATP Masters 1000 final. Gauff, who won the 2023 title beating Karolina Muchova and then went on to win her first Grand Slam at the US Open, stormed to a 5-0 lead in the first set before winning it 6-2. Pegula battled back to 5-4 in the second before Gauff closed out the win. Gauff won five of six break points. The last time two American women played in the Cincinnati final was in 1970, when Rosie Casals beat Nancy Richey. Pegula’s best finish in Cincinnati came in 2024, when she lost to Aryna Sabalenka in the final. In Saturday’s semifinals, Pegula beat defending champion Iga Swiatek and Gauff defeated Sara Bejlek to set up the first all-American women’s final at the Cincinnati Open in 56 years. “I think it was a long journey, but I’m happy,” Gauff said after the match. “I think it’s night and day, the player I was last year to now. I don’t think that this is an indicator that I’m going to do well in New York.

stories.title: Ceferin won’t challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency but tells him to quit
stories.summary: European football chief doesn’t want to lose credibility over FIFA job but says Infantino will face a challenger. European football chief Aleksander Ceferin says he is “not interested” in replacing Gianni Infantino but warned the under-fire FIFA president must quit or face a leadership challenge. Ceferin has been vocal in his criticism since Infantino revealed his controversial plans to seek private investment in a company to run FIFA tournaments. However, ruling himself out of a bid to take Infantino’s place, the 58-year-old Slovenian told. The Rest is Politics podcast on Monday that he is “not interested because of two reasons”. “One reason is that I love UEFA and I love working here, and I think that at a certain point… it’s time to also enjoy life a bit,” he said. “And the second point is, my credibility is much, much higher if I’m not interested in the position.” Infantino has come under increasing pressure to step down as head of world football’s governing body over his now-abandoned plan to secure private investment in FIFA tournaments, including the World Cup. UEFA, which oversees European football, has threatened a boycott of FIFA competitions, with several continental and national federations also withdrawing their support for Infantino. Ceferin now believes Infantino’s previously impregnable position is under threat, with him forecasting the Swiss will have to stand down or face a leadership challenge if he seeks re-election at the next FIFA Congress in Morocco in March. Infantino, a former UEFA secretary-general, had the broad backing of European nations when he succeeded Sepp Blatter as FIFA president in 2016. But Ceferin, who revealed he has not spoken to Infantino since the controversy started, insisted the current situation was very different.
